title: Boxplots and outliers
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:39Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The outlier rule appears in mat-shape-distribution, but that card is mainly about distribution shape, and mat-spread-box-plots says whiskers reach the lowest and highest scores, which conflicts with drawing outliers as separate points, so neither card teaches this point as briefed.

draft.title: Boxplots and outliers
card: The IQR is Q3 − Q1. An outlier is a value below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. These two numbers are the fences.
Example: Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 32. The IQR is 12 and 1.5 × 12 = 18. The fences are 20 − 18 = 2 and 32 + 18 = 50.
A value exactly on a fence is not an outlier. It must be beyond the fence, so 50 is not an outlier but 51 is.
On a boxplot, outliers are drawn as separate points. The whiskers stop at the smallest and largest values that are not outliers.
draft.remember: Find the IQR, build the fences with 1.5 × IQR, and plot anything beyond them as a point.

a.q: A data set has Q1 = 40 and Q3 = 52. What is the upper fence for outliers?
a.why: IQR = 52 − 40 = 12, and 1.5 × 12 = 18. The upper fence is 52 + 18 = 70. Adding only the IQR gives 64, which skips the 1.5.

b.q: A boxplot of daily bike hires has Q1 = 15 and Q3 = 27. Which value would be drawn as a separate point?
b.why: IQR = 12, so the upper fence is 27 + 18 = 45. Only 46 is above it. The value 45 is on the fence, so it is not an outlier.
b.clue: A value on the fence is not beyond it.

check.summary: No problems found. The fences, the strict 'beyond the fence' rule and the whisker convention match the VCE General Mathematics treatment, and both answers (70 and 46) check out.
